# Kanji mode encoding for Standard QR, Micro QR and rMQR

## Purpose

Phase 6 of [featherqr-2.0.0-plan.md](featherqr-2.0.0-plan.md). All three decoders read Kanji mode and no generator writes it ([qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md), "Why Kanji mode is read but never written"), so Japanese text goes out as UTF-8 in Byte mode: 24 bits for a kana or a kanji where Kanji mode spends 13, plus a 12-bit ECI header. A Standard QR 40-L symbol holds 1,817 characters in Kanji mode and 984 as UTF-8; Micro QR M4-L holds 9 against 5, and M3-L 6 against 3. Micro QR has a second reason: it has no ECI, so its UTF-8 Byte output reads as Japanese only in a reader that guesses UTF-8, while Kanji mode is the standard's own way to carry the text.

This plan fixes WHAT ships, in WHICH order, and WHY each rule is what it is. HOW each piece is verified follows the mandatory test-first workflow. The code-level inventory it was written from (insertion points, the premises that stop holding, the tests and statements that move) is in [references/kanji-encoding-inventory.md](references/kanji-encoding-inventory.md). When the plan completes, its durable content graduates into [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md), the three encoder records and spec maps and [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](../specs/qrcode-test-fixtures.md); the 2.0.0 plan's Phase 6 row gets its Progress log entry, and this file and its reference are deleted.

## Scope

| In | Out |
|---|---|
| Kanji segments written by all three generators, in single mode and under `Optimal` segmentation | Kanji beside an ECI header (D6). A text with a character that is neither ASCII nor encodable in Kanji mode stays entirely UTF-8 in the first cut; phase 6.7 extends this only if the oracle sweep allows it |
| Structured Append sets (Standard QR) | Shift_JIS written as Byte mode or under ECI 20. The encoder still writes only Latin-1 and UTF-8 bytes, so the reasoning of D7 in the parent plan stands; the ECI 20 decode scope row is untouched |
| A reverse table generated from the sweep that produced `ShiftJisKanjiTable` | CP932's characters: NEC row 13, the IBM extensions, halfwidth katakana, and the CP932 readings of the seven divergent cells. They have no cell to write, and reading them is already out of scope (`UnmappedCharacter`) |
| Sizing (`TryGetRequiredBufferSize`), refusal messages, the capacity documentation | A public option to turn Kanji off. `EciMode.Utf8` already does it on Standard QR and rMQR. Micro QR has no charset option, and a switch for it waits for a concrete request (the public API growth rule) |
| Oracle cross-checks and committed fixtures covering every Kanji count-indicator width of every symbology | Changing the `Segmentation` default. Japanese text with ASCII in it (URLs, order numbers) reaches Kanji only under `Optimal`; making `Optimal` the default is its own decision |
| The segmenter's lane kernels, if measurement says they are needed (6.8) | The 128-bit tiers for the kernels this plan changes (parent plan, Phase 6b). They wait for this plan; see "Relation to other work" |

## When a text is written in Kanji mode

A text is **eligible** when both of these hold:

1. The library chose the charset itself, and it chose UTF-8. That means `EciMode.Default` (always the case on Micro QR), a character above U+00FF in the text, and on Standard QR `Utf8Bom` off.
2. Every character is either ASCII or has an **encoder cell**: a JIS X 0208 cell whose reading is not one of the seven that CP932 reads differently (K3).

Every text that is not eligible is written exactly as today, bit for bit.

| Text | `Single` | `Optimal` |
|---|---|---|
| ASCII or Latin-1 | As today | As today |
| `EciMode.Iso8859_1` or `EciMode.Utf8` set, or `Utf8Bom` on | As today: a charset the caller chose is honoured | As today |
| Eligible, and every character has a cell (「日本語」, 「脂至肢」) | One Kanji segment, no ECI | The same stream: one Kanji run is the program's optimum |
| Eligible, with ASCII in it (「QRコード」, 「日本7777」) | Today's UTF-8 Byte stream, because one segment cannot hold both | Kanji runs beside Numeric, Alphanumeric and Byte runs of ASCII, with no ECI. Taken when it lowers the version, as any plan is today |
| Has a non-ASCII character with no cell (é, emoji, ～ U+FF5E, ① U+2460, ｶ U+FF76, 〜 U+301C) | As today | As today, until 6.7 |
| Micro QR with the version range limited to M1-M2 | As today (Kanji exists from M3) | As today |

**Why "only where UTF-8 would have been written".** ASCII and Latin-1 output never moves, so the change reaches exactly the texts that cost the most today. Every non-ASCII character with a cell costs 16 or 24 bits in UTF-8 against 13 in Kanji mode, so wherever the rule applies, Kanji is the cheaper encoding character for character. The one cell cheaper in Byte mode, U+005C, is ASCII and one of the seven, so it is never written as Kanji. A single-mode Kanji stream also drops the ECI header.

**Why no ECI.** A text whose Byte runs carry only ASCII needs no ECI header at all. That avoids D6's open question (does every reader apply JIS X 0208 to a Kanji segment that follows ECI 26?). This library's decoder does, but no test covers it and no other reader's behaviour has been recorded. It also keeps Structured Append parity well defined: the bytes an eligible text carries are its Shift_JIS encoding whatever the plan, so the parity does not depend on how the text is segmented (K6).

**The cost this rule accepts.** Japanese text typed on Windows often carries CP932 readings (～ U+FF5E, － U+FF0D, ￠ ￡ ￢, ∥) or NEC characters (①, ㈱), and Japanese text from other sources often carries halfwidth katakana. Any one of them keeps the whole text in UTF-8. Phase 6.7 is where that limit is lifted, if it can be.

## Structured Append

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| A set is eligible when the whole text is. An eligible set carries no ECI header in any symbol | One charset per set, as today ([standardqr-encoder.md](../specs/standardqr-encoder.md#structured-append)) |
| The parity of an eligible set is the XOR of the whole text's Shift_JIS bytes, ASCII characters taken as their single byte. It is computed once, before splitting | Those bytes do not depend on the plan, so the "computed once" rule survives. For the corpus sentence 「こんにちは世界、QRコードの分割テストです。」×3 this gives 176, the value CodeGlyphX writes in its Kanji-mode set; QrCodeGenerator's UTF-8 set of the same text carries 6 |
| Under `Single` segmentation, an eligible set is written in Kanji mode only when every character has a cell. Otherwise the set is today's UTF-8 set | Every chunk must be one segment, and a chunk holding both kana and ASCII cannot be one Kanji segment |
| Under `Optimal`, the Kanji set is compared to today's UTF-8 set the way `Create` compares a plan with the single stream. It is taken only when it needs fewer symbols, or the same number at a lower version | `Optimal` must never give a larger set than today's. The balanced-split rules apply unchanged inside either set |
| Inside a Kanji set, a chunk has no UTF-8 fallback; its stream is its Kanji plan | The set carries one charset |
| A text that fits in one symbol still returns `Create`'s symbol, byte for byte | As today |
| The cost model learns Kanji. A text's single mode can now be Kanji; the closed-form chunk end gains a Kanji prefix; the lower bound prices a character with a cell at 13 bits | Two premises stop holding in the eligible path: that a text's single mode changes at most twice along it (Numeric, Alphanumeric, Byte), and that a character outside the alphanumeric alphabet extends only a Byte run |

This closes the encoder record's decision that the parity follows the bytes ([standardqr-encoder.md](../specs/standardqr-encoder.md#decisions)): the encoder-side Japanese parity cases are added in 6.5.

## Decisions

| # | Decision | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| K1 | When is Kanji considered? | **Recommended:** the eligibility rule above. It refines the parent plan's D5 escape hatch: an explicit `EciMode`, or `Utf8Bom`, keeps today's stream |
| K2 | Does single mode pick Kanji automatically? (D5) | **Yes**, when every character has a cell, with a migration note. This is the parent plan's recommendation, and 6.3 confirms it |
| K3 | The seven cells CP932 reads differently (0x815F, 0x8160, 0x8161, 0x817C, 0x8191, 0x8192, 0x81CA) | **Never written**; neither of their readings has an encoder cell. This library reads 0x8160 as U+301C, and a CP932 reader such as ZXing.Net reads it as U+FF5E. Writing either reading at that cell would make a symbol that two readers decode differently, and writing U+FF5E would also break this library's own round trip. The parent plan's claim that "falls through to Byte" makes the divergence a non-issue for encoding held only for the CP932 readings, which have no reverse entry; the JIS X 0208 readings would have had one |
| K4 | Kanji segments beside ECI-tagged Byte segments (D6) | **Not in the first cut.** 6.6 measures the readers, and 6.7 decides from what they show |
| K5 | Micro QR | **The same rule, with no option.** Kanji is the more interoperable form there, because Micro QR has no ECI. It is available from M3 |
| K6 | Structured Append parity with Kanji | **The XOR of the whole text's Shift_JIS bytes**, per the table above |
| K7 | Non-Japanese scripts in JIS X 0208 (Greek, Cyrillic, box drawing, Latin-1 symbols) | **Recommended: eligible.** The rule is about what can be represented, not about script, so the single word 「Привет」 becomes one Kanji segment (13 bits a letter against 16). The 6.6 sweep over every encoder cell is the check. A row that any pinned reader misreads loses its cells |
| K8 | Reverse table | **Generated** from `kanji-sweep.tsv` by the generator that writes `ShiftJisKanjiTable`. The generator refuses unless the reverse table is the exact inverse of the forward one over the 6,872 encoder cells. It is RVA data: no allocation, no static constructor, no `System.Text.Encoding.CodePages`. The target size is no larger than the forward table's 16 KB. The representation is chosen in 6.1 by measured lookup time and size, and the trimmed-size delta is recorded beside the sizes in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md) |
| K9 | The segmenter's lane kernels (Vector256 and AdvSimd, and the Structured Append lane walks) | **Eligible texts take the scalar program** until 6.8 measures the lanes. Other texts keep the lanes unchanged |

## What has to stay true

- **Non-eligible text is byte-identical** in all three symbologies under every option. This covers `Create` (both overloads), `CreateStructuredAppend`, `TryGetRequiredBufferSize` and the refusal messages. It is checked through the public API against the previous commit, on the existing corpora plus a random one.
- **`Decode(Encode(x)) == x` for every eligible text**, in this library and in every pinned reader of the symbology. The asymmetry recorded in the spec ("`Encode(Decode(y))` does not reproduce a Kanji symbol") then holds only for symbols this plan does not write.
- **`PublicAPI.approved.txt` does not change.** `EncodingMode` is internal and gains `Kanji`; only XML docs change.
- **The existing parity suites pass unchanged** (`ModeSegmenter*ParityTest` and the `StructuredAppend*` walks and scans), because the programs they pin are the ones non-eligible text still runs.
- **Speed.** The benchmark arms of non-eligible text stay within noise. An arm whose output moves does different work now, so it is not held to the +10 % rule. It is reported next to the same text with `EciMode.Utf8` forced (today's path), and it must be no slower than that.

## Design

What each piece is. Where it goes in the code is in the inventory.

- **Mode.** `EncodingMode.Kanji` uses Standard QR's indicator (`1000`), as the other members do. Micro QR writes `11` on M3 and `011` on M4, and rMQR writes `100`. The count-indicator widths already exist for decoding: Standard QR 8/10/12, Micro QR 3/4, rMQR 2 to 7. Micro QR's mode availability gains Kanji from M3.
- **Writers.** Each symbology's single-segment and segmented writers gain a 13-bit writer. Adding an arm to a hot `switch` has moved the other arms before (a fourth arm in the Micro QR decoder cost the M2 numeric and M4 byte benchmarks 12-15 %, and rMQR keeps its writers in one `switch` for that reason), so each writer is measured for what it does to the arms it does not touch.
- **Version selection and capacity.** Standard QR's capacity table already carries a Kanji column that nothing reads. rMQR's precomputed fit table grows by one mode. Micro QR's required-bits arithmetic learns the 13-bit rate.
- **Segmenter.** An eighth state, enabled only for eligible text, so every other program is today's. In the eligible path, ASCII characters behave as they do today; a character with a cell reaches only the Kanji state, because Byte would need an ECI. The lower bounds and shortcuts that assume a character outside the alphanumeric alphabet extends only a Byte run are re-derived for the eligible path. There are about a dozen of them across the three planners and the Structured Append walks (listed in the inventory), and each is a place where a wrong bound would silently skip a winning plan.
- **Analysis.** The eligibility pass runs only after the analysis has resolved UTF-8, and stops at the first character without a cell. ASCII and Latin-1 input never pays for it.

## Phases

Each phase follows the test-first workflow, updates the affected specs and `docs/migration.md` in the same change, and appends a Progress log entry with Done / Lessons / benchmark delta. `PublicAPI.approved.txt` stays unchanged, and a diff there is a defect. Phases that move a hot path measure it the way the Standard QR writer plan does: a worktree at the previous commit against the change, the same benchmark file, three rounds alternating, and the untouched arms read as the noise of the day. The sub-phases are numbered, not lettered, because the parent plan's Phase 6b is the 128-bit tiers.

| # | Priority | Phase | Contents | Exit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | **P0** | Reverse table | Generator extension (K8), K3's exclusions, lookup variants measured | The reverse table is the exact inverse of the forward one over 6,872 cells; the seven cells, rows 9-15 and rows 85-94 have no entry; the golden digest is pinned; size and lookup time are recorded. Internal only, and no generator output changes |
| 6.2 | **P0** | Writers and version selection, dark | `EncodingMode.Kanji`; the writers in all three encoders, single and segmented; count widths; capacity and fit tables. Reachable from tests only | Streams equal an independent reference written from the standard's definition, at every count-indicator width of every symbology and at every starting bit alignment of a segmented run. Capacity at every version and level equals the standard's Kanji column: Standard QR from the table in `QRCodeConstants`, Micro QR from ISO/IEC 18004, rMQR from ISO/IEC 23941. Round trip through the three matrix decoders. The non-Kanji arms of `SimpleEncode` and `*EncodeEndToEnd` stay within noise |
| 6.3 | **P0** | Single mode flips (K1, K2, K5) | Eligibility in the analysis; the three generators, sizing and refusal messages; migration note; golden images that move (e.g. `Create_Default_PixelsMatchSample("脂至肢")`, while its `Utf8` twin does not) are regenerated deliberately | One test per class of the eligibility truth table (`EciMode` × `Utf8Bom` × text class × symbology × version range), negatives included. Non-eligible corpus byte-identical. ZXing.Net decodes, in CI, Standard QR output covering every encoder cell. zxing-cpp reads the Micro QR and rMQR output through the tool's spot checks |
| 6.4 | P1 | `Optimal` (K9) | The eighth state; the three planners; the re-derived bounds; eligible texts kept off the lanes | Parity against an independent eight-state reference. The seven-state suites unchanged. For every re-derived bound, a test where the old bound would have skipped the winning plan. `Optimal` never larger than `Single`. Round trip |
| 6.5 | P1 | Structured Append (K6) | The rules above; the chunk cost model; the parity | For the CodeGlyphX set's text, `Optimal` writes parity 176 and `Single` still writes 6. Round trip. Every symbol shares one version and one parity. The balanced bound holds. A one-symbol result equals `Create`. The Structured Append arms are reported against forced UTF-8 |
| 6.6 | P1 | Interop and fixtures | A ZXing.Net Standard QR Kanji fixture in the 12-bit band (versions 27-40). qrtool rMQR Kanji fixtures at count widths 2, 3 and 6, compared module for module (rMQR has one mask, so matrix equality is a valid encoder oracle there); this closes the widths [rmqr-encoder.md](../specs/rmqr-encoder.md) says rest on derivation alone. Every encoder cell through zxing-cpp (all three symbologies) and ZXing.Net (Standard QR). ASCII `\` and `~` in Byte runs beside Kanji runs (a JIS X 0201 reader shows ¥ and ‾). A Kanji segment after ECI 26, read by each reader, as evidence for 6.7. A spot-check list for the Phase 8 checklist | Every reader agrees with the input on every cell it is asked about, or the row goes (K7). Fixtures committed with provenance. Tag `2.0.0-preview.4` (the parent plan's Phase 6 exit) |
| 6.7 | P2 | Kanji beside UTF-8 ECI (D6) | Only if 6.6 shows every pinned reader applies JIS X 0208 to a Kanji segment after ECI 26. It needs its own parity rule, since the carried bytes then depend on the plan | Its own truth table and sweep. It moves output that 6.3-6.5 left alone, so it ships in 2.0.0 or waits for the next major, not a minor |
| 6.8 | P2 | Lanes (K9) and Kanji plan speed | The segmenter lanes and the Structured Append lane walks gain the Kanji state, but only if the scalar path misses the "no slower than forced UTF-8" bar. Also the per-run cost of a Kanji plan on interleaved text, where 6.4 missed that bar on rMQR (+20 %) and Micro QR (+30 % against the build before Kanji plans): the scan's cost run reused for the build, and one reverse-table lookup per character instead of one in the analysis and another in the writer | The measurement recorded either way. It lands before the release if the bar is missed, which 6.4 found it is |
| 6.9 | P1 | Fold | Specs; `README.md` (the mode table, the encoding FAQ, the decode-only notes); `docs/data-capacity.md` (Kanji columns; the UTF-8 columns lose 'あ' as their test character, since it is now written as Kanji); `docs/migration.md`; XML docs; the Playground API page regenerated; the index | The specs carry the rules and decisions, and nothing is left only here. The plan and its reference are deleted |

6.1 and 6.2 land dark: no generator writes Kanji until 6.3. The flips are 6.3 to 6.5, and **no tag is cut between the first flip and the last**. So no release has `Create` writing Kanji while `CreateStructuredAppend` writes UTF-8 for the same text, or has `Single` and `Optimal` disagreeing about which texts can be Kanji. 6.6 closes the P0/P1 work with the preview tag. 6.7 can be dropped without reopening anything else. 6.8 could have been, but 6.4 missed its speed bar on rMQR and Micro QR, so it now has work that lands before the release.

## Relation to other work

- **Parent decisions.** K2 answers D5 and K4 answers the first half of D6. D7 stands, because Kanji is a mode, not a charset, and the encoder still writes no ECI 20. **Decided 2026-09-29: this plan ships in 2.0.0, and 2.1.0 is not an option.** It changes default output, which D5 accepts in a major only, so a slip delays Phase 8 rather than moving the plan. That makes the P0 and P1 phases (6.1-6.6 and 6.9) release blockers. Only 6.7 and 6.8 can be dropped: 6.7 then waits for the next major, since it moves output too, and 6.8 is needed only if its bar is missed, which 6.4 found it is (rMQR and Micro QR Kanji plans on interleaved text).
- **128-bit tiers (parent Phase 6b).** `ModeSegmenterLanes`, `TextAnalyzer`, `StructuredAppendScanner`, `StructuredAppendParity` and `StructuredAppendLanes` wait for 6.4 and 6.5: this plan changes their state set, their analysis and their parity bytes. The other kernels of 6b are unaffected and can proceed in parallel. 6b's encode-side ranking is taken after 6.5 lands, since the share of each kernel moves.
- **Benchmarks whose output moves.** The `Optimal` arms of `QRCodeSegmentationEncode` `utf8-60`, `RmQRSegmentationEncode` `utf8-60` and `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode` `utf8-15k-*`. Their `Single` arms carry ASCII, so they do not move and serve as controls. New shapes: a text in which every character has a cell, per symbology, under `Single`.

## Verification notes

- The reference writer is built in the test from the standard's definition, not from the library's table: the Shift_JIS pair taken from `kanji-sweep.tsv`, minus 0x8140 or 0xC140, high byte × 0xC0 plus low byte, 13 bits MSB first.
- Mutation checks with `tools/mutation_check.cs`: each clause of the eligibility rule, each of the seven exclusions, the 13-bit width, the two offsets and the multiplier, every symbology's mode indicator and count width, Micro QR's M3 floor, the source of the parity bytes, and every re-derived bound. Each must fail a test.
- Matrix equality is a valid encoder oracle on rMQR only. On Standard QR and Micro QR the mask choice differs between encoders, so they are checked through readers, and through data codewords where the stream has only one valid form (a single Kanji segment at a fixed version and level).
- The byte-identical comparison prints which tree each side loaded.
- By hand in the Playground: encode Japanese in each symbology, check the decode preview and the share-link round trip. The Phase 8 physical-scanner pass is already weighted toward Kanji.

## Progress log

Entries are appended per phase: what was done, what was learned, and the benchmark delta or an explicit statement that no hot path moved.

### 6.1 Reverse table (2026-09-29)

**Done.** `generate-kanji-table` now also emits `src/FeatherQR/Internals/ShiftJisKanjiReverseTable.cs` (`ReverseTable` in `tools/QRInteropFixtures/KanjiReverseTable.cs`), built from the validated forward table rather than from the sweep a second time, so the two cannot come from different data. Both tables are validated before either is written. The gate runs the emitted lookup on the emitted bytes over all 65,536 code units: the exact inverse of the forward table without the seven cells, 6,872 hits, and both readings of each of the seven (the JIS X 0208 one and the CP932 one) miss. `ShiftJisKanjiReverseTableUnitTest` repeats that against the shipped forward table and adds the ASCII range, NEC row 13, the IBM extensions, halfwidth katakana, JIS X 0201's ¥ and ‾, surrogates, the unassigned rows, 15 spot cells across the scripts and both Kanji-mode ranges, and a golden digest over every lookup. Nothing outside the tests references the table; `PublicAPI.approved.txt` is unchanged. `tools/mutation_check.cs` planted 20 faults in the lookup, and each one failed at least three test methods: six slips in the lookup itself (the membership test, the rank's mask, the 13-bit shift, mask and stride, the block index) and each of the 14 readings of the seven cells mapped back to its cell. A remark in `ShiftJisKanjiTableUnitTest` that still named `UnsupportedContent` now names `UnmappedCharacter`.

**Measured** (self-contained BenchmarkDotNet harness outside the repo, .NET 10, x64; the correctness gate compared every variant with an inversion of the forward table over all 65,536 code units before any timing). Per character, 1,000 characters of Japanese prose / the 6,872 cells shuffled:

| Layout | Bytes | Prose | All cells |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sorted pairs, binary search | 27,488 | 14.2 ns | 37 ns |
| Hash and displace, 16-bit seeds, checked through the forward table | 14,034 (+ forward) | 7.3 ns | 5.6 ns |
| Directory + word + rank in separate arrays, 16-bit values | 17,720 | 2.9-3.0 ns | 2.4-2.7 ns |
| The same, 13-bit values | 15,146 | 2.8-3.4 ns | 2.7-3.2 ns |
| The same, rank per 256-code-unit page | 14,588 | 4.1 ns | 3.6 ns |
| **Directory + fused 10-byte record + 13-bit values (shipped)** | **15,146** | **2.2-3.3 ns** | **2.4-2.8 ns** |
| The shipped layout without bounds checks | 15,146 | 2.0 ns | 2.3 ns |

Ranges are two runs (the second with three launches); compare within a run.

**Lessons.**

- The perfect hash lost although it is the smallest: two multiply-heavy hashes plus a load into the 16 KB forward table cost more than the bitmap's directory, record and value loads. With 8-bit seeds it did not build at all at any load factor tried (a bucket of 3 to 5 found no free slots in 256 seeds once half the table was full); 16-bit seeds at λ = 5 do.
- Fusing the word and its rank into one record is what makes 13-bit packing free: with separate arrays packing cost 3-27 %, with the record it is level with the unpacked 16-bit layout on the shuffled cells and within run-to-run noise of it on prose (9 % behind in one run, 26 % ahead in the other), and that layout misses the 16 KB target anyway.
- The committed forward file had drifted from its generator: its comments had been reflowed to one sentence per line by hand and the template had not. Regeneration therefore rewrote 31 lines of comments with no data change. The template now matches, and regeneration reproduces the committed file byte for byte; a hand edit to a generated file has to go into the generator too.
- The trimmed-size delta cannot be measured yet, since trimming removes an unreferenced table. It is recorded when 6.3 first references the table.

**Benchmark delta.** No hot path moved: no production code references the new table, and the forward table is byte-identical.

### 6.2 Writers and version selection, dark (2026-09-29)

**Done.** `EncodingMode.Kanji` (8, Standard QR's `1000`) and `ModeSegment` index 3. Every single-segment and segmented writer of the three symbologies gained a Kanji arm that writes the reverse table's 13-bit value, two characters to one 26-bit append. Standard QR's count widths are 8/10/12 through `GetCountIndicatorLength`. Micro QR has indicator 3, a count of `version` bits, and Kanji in `IsModeSupported` from M3. rMQR has indicator `100`, mode index 3 with `ModeCount` 4, and one more mode in the fit table (48 capacity rows instead of 36). The required-bit arithmetic of all three, `ModeSegmenter.PayloadBits` and the planners' `MeasurePlan` price Kanji at 13 bits a character. The rMQR arm sits in `EncodeDataCodewordsWithoutEci` only: Kanji has no ECI, so the ECI writer rejects it through its existing default arm. `TextAnalyzer` is untouched, so no generator selects Kanji and every output is unchanged; `PublicAPI.approved.txt` is unchanged.

The writers refuse two things rather than write them. A character without a cell is caught after the loop from the OR of the lookups (a miss is -1 and still occupies its 13 bits, so the unchecked rMQR and Micro QR stores stay inside capacity), and `KanjiCells` scans for its name on the failure path only. A Kanji run under an ECI header is refused by Standard QR's single-segment and segmented writers and by rMQR's segmented writer (K4). Micro QR has no ECI, so it has no second refusal.

**Verified.** `KanjiStreamReference` writes streams from the standards with nothing taken from the library: the Shift_JIS pair from .NET's CP932 encoder, compacted as ISO/IEC 18004 8.4.5 states it, and count widths transcribed from the published tables. `QRBinaryEncoderKanjiTest`, `MicroQRBinaryEncoderKanjiTest` and `RmQRBinaryEncoderKanjiTest` check against it:
- the single-segment writer filled to capacity at every version and level (all 160 Standard QR symbols, every length of the five Micro QR Kanji symbols, all 64 rMQR symbols), so every count width is written at its largest count;
- all 6,872 cells through each symbology's writer;
- a Kanji run starting at every bit offset modulo 64 (Standard QR in each count band, rMQR), and on Micro QR at every residue modulo 8 and at every start from bit 52 to 64, across the 128-bit accumulator's word boundary;
- a one-run plan equal to the single-segment stream, and the refusals;
- capacity at every version and level equal to the Kanji column: Standard QR's table in `QRCodeConstants`, ISO/IEC 18004 Table 7 for Micro QR, the published transcription of ISO/IEC 23941 Table 7 for rMQR; rMQR's precomputed auto-fit equal to a definitional scan for every Kanji count under all three strategies;
- a round trip through the three matrix decoders, the symbols assembled from the generators' internal stages, since no generator writes Kanji yet.

`tools/mutation_check.cs` planted 22 faults (each count width, the 13-bit width and the pair order in each writer, each mode indicator, Micro QR's M3 floor and count, rMQR's mode index and a Kanji width row, the 13-bit price in the fit arithmetic and in `PayloadBits`, `ModeSegment`'s index, the miss test and each ECI refusal), and the Kanji test classes caught every one. The two ECI refusals and rMQR's are caught by one method each, the tests written for them.

**Lessons.**

- rMQR's Kanji widths 2, 3 and 6 now have a second reading. The Wikipedia transcription of ISO/IEC 23941 Table 3 agrees with all 128 widths, and its Table 7 agrees with the Kanji capacity those widths give on 63 of 64 cells. The 64th, R11x77-M, is a corrupt row whose Numeric, Alphanumeric and Byte cells are R11x59-H's, so a published table is a second reading, not an oracle on its own.
- CP932 is a usable reference for every encoder cell, the characters CP932 also places in NEC row 13 (∵, ≒, ≡ and others) included: .NET's encoder writes the JIS X 0208 cell for them, or the every-cell tests would have failed.
- The inlined Kanji arm made Micro QR's `EncodeDataCodewords` 3,983 → 5,168 bytes of Tier-1 code (43 → 73 PGO inlinees) without adding a call or a spill to the hot arms, and the arms did not move. A reachable Kanji arm in 6.3 may change that picture.
- The first A/B was void. In two rounds the head tree came out 50-87 % slower on nearly every arm, including ones no Kanji code reaches (Micro QR numeric M2 140 → 244 ns), yet an interleaved probe on an idle machine (two launches, fifteen iterations) put base and head level on the same arms, and the rerun above agrees. What slowed those head passes was not found. A second trap came out of stopping it: stopping the A/B's background task left its script running, so the next probes shared the machine with the third round until the process tree was killed. Before an A/B starts, check that no earlier benchmark process is alive, and read an arm that the change cannot reach as the noise of that run.

**Benchmark delta.** Base `27a5caf` against this change, both trees exported outside the repository, ShortRun, three rounds alternating on an idle machine, median of the three means per arm, 102 arms: the FeatherQR arms of `SimpleEncode`, `SimpleMicroQREncode` and `SimpleRmQREncode`, all of `QRCodeEncodeEndToEnd`, `MicroQREncodeEndToend` and `RmQREncodeEndToEnd`, and the three `*SegmentationEncode` classes, since the segmented writers changed too. Allocation is identical to the byte on every arm. Median delta per class: `SimpleEncode` -0.2 %, `SimpleMicroQREncode` +0.2 %, `SimpleRmQREncode` -3.2 %, `QRCodeEncodeEndToEnd` +0.2 %, `MicroQREncodeEndToend` +0.1 %, `RmQREncodeEndToEnd` -0.4 %, and +0.6 to +0.9 % for the segmentation classes; the overall median is +0.4 %, and no arm moved past +10 % (range -19.7 % to +9.0 %). Two arms were high in all three rounds, and both were measured again with three launches of fifteen iterations, interleaved twice. `RmQR_Numeric_R7x43_Encode` (+8 % in the A/B) came out +2 % in both its classes, the same call through `SimpleRmQREncode` included (153-157 → 156-160 ns), so most of the A/B figure was per-process layout. rMQR `Optimal` leans up over its twelve shapes (median +3.1 %, range -5.0 to +8.4 %) where rMQR `Single` does not (median -0.3 %), which fits a small real cost in the segmented writer's per-run arms or the count-width switch that gained a case. It is inside the +10 % rule; 6.4 reworks that planner and measures it again.

### 6.3 Single mode flips (2026-09-29)

**Done.** `TextAnalyzer.Analyze(text, eci, allowKanji)` runs the analysis unchanged, then, only when the charset was the library's choice and came out UTF-8, a pass that stops at the first character without an encoder cell; a text that passes is `(Kanji, no ECI, character count)`. The two-argument `Analyze` keeps every caller it had and every test that pins it. Standard QR opts in on its single-symbol paths (sizing, the version and boost resolution, the encode, both `Optimal` entries) with `allowKanji: !Utf8Bom`; Micro QR and rMQR opt in everywhere. Structured Append keeps the old analysis for the set, so a set of more than one symbol is still UTF-8, and a text that fits one symbol goes through `Create` and comes out Kanji. The three planners treat a Kanji analysis as already optimal, as they treat Numeric (`QRSegmentPlanner.CanPlanBeatSingleMode` is now Alphanumeric or Byte only; the Micro QR and rMQR planners return early): a Kanji analysis carries no charset, and priced under none its characters would look like narrowed Latin-1 bytes. Refusals count Kanji in characters, and Micro QR's mode-availability wording names Kanji only when the refused mode is Kanji. The generators' class docs, `EciMode.Default`/`Utf8` and the `EciMode`/`Utf8Bom` options say what is written, the Playground API page is regenerated, and `docs/migration.md` has "Japanese text is written in Kanji mode". Specs: the architecture's "Why Kanji mode is read but never written" became "When Kanji mode is written", and the decoder, encoder and spec-map statements that said decode only are updated. `PublicAPI.approved.txt` is unchanged.

**Verified.**
- `KanjiEligibilityTest`, one test per class of the truth table through the public API, every expectation a whole symbol built from a `KanjiStreamReference` stream with the mask pinned. The reference gained ECI headers and UTF-8 runs, so "as today" is asserted as exactly as "Kanji", and every "as today" case passed before the change. All-cells text is one Kanji segment under `Single` and `Optimal` on all three symbologies (kana, kanji, Cyrillic, Greek, box drawing, Latin-1 symbols beside kanji, fullwidth forms, punctuation); with a byte order mark or explicit UTF-8 it stays UTF-8; eligible text with ASCII stays UTF-8 under `Single`, and `Optimal` writes today's UTF-8 plan; a character without a cell (é, emoji, both readings of a divergent cell, ①, halfwidth katakana, ㈱, an IBM extension) and Latin-1 text stay as they were; the empty text too. Also: an exact version only Kanji fits now holds the text, sizing matches `Create` under every mode-deciding option, the boost prices the Kanji stream, the version-40 refusal counts Kanji characters, a one-symbol set is `Create`'s Kanji symbol, Micro QR limited to M1-M2 refuses as before, and the capacity refusals of Micro QR and rMQR count characters.
- ZXing.Net reads every encoder cell from `Create`'s output, in all three count bands (`KanjiZXingCrossTest`, in CI). ZXing.Net needs the code-pages provider for Shift_JIS; the test assembly registers it in a module initializer, so every ZXing.Net test in the process runs with it whatever the order, and none changed.
- zxing-cpp through the tool: `spot-check-rmqr` now also writes the largest all-cells text every version and level holds and requires zxing-cpp's raw bytes to be its Shift_JIS encoding, which proves the symbol is Kanji mode: 382 of 382, 64 of them Kanji, every count width 2-7. `spot-check-microqr` gained five Kanji cases at the M3 and M4 boundaries and a UTF-8 one: 14 of 14.
- Byte-identical: a harness built against each tree (the previous commit `c7ee3aa` and this change, both exported, each run printing the assembly path and MVID it loaded) ran 38,314 cases over 545 texts (fixed ones plus a seeded random corpus) through `Create` both overloads, `TryGetRequiredBufferSize`, `CreateStructuredAppend` and every refusal message, with the text class decided from `kanji-sweep.tsv` rather than the library. ASCII, Latin-1, empty, eligible-with-ASCII and no-cell text: 0 differences in 28,258 cases. All-cells text changed only where the Kanji path applies: explicit charset and byte order mark cases 0 of 2,253, multi-symbol sets 0 of 105, one-symbol sets on the Kanji path 70 of 70. No text that fit stopped fitting, 715 fit now that did not, and no Standard QR version grew.
- Existing tests that pinned UTF-8 output for Japanese text were decided one by one. Tests about UTF-8 capacity (`Create_ExactBoundary_ByteUtf8`, `Create_MaxByte_FitsInVersion40` and its span twin) now ask for UTF-8; `GeneratorOptionsTest`'s released-output row for 「日本語のテキスト」 asks for UTF-8 and still reproduces the released hash; rMQR's auto-detect test uses 「こんにちは世界～」, which has no Kanji form; Micro QR's round trip expects M3 for 「こんにちは」 and gained a 9-Kanji M4 case and a 15-byte UTF-8 one; rMQR's exhaustive version reference learned the Kanji single stream. `Create_ExactBoundary_Kanji` pins the Kanji column through the public API at every band edge.
- `tools/mutation_check.cs` planted 14 faults (each clause of the eligibility test, the stop at a missing cell, the character count, the byte order mark and sizing and boost opt-ins, each planner's Kanji early return, both refusal units and the Micro QR wording condition); all are caught. The rMQR planner's return was not caught at first, because the Optimal test pinned the version and a pinned version never reaches the planner; `RmQr_AllCellsAutoFit_OptimalIsTheSingleKanjiSymbol` catches it.

**Lessons.**
- No golden image moved. The inventory expected `Create_Default_PixelsMatchSample("脂至肢")` to, but that literal is `脂至肢`: mojibake left three private-use characters between the kanji, which no editor shows and which have no cell. The other Japanese literals in that class are mojibake with halfwidth katakana, as the inventory said.
- The byte-identical harness caught what the tests did not: the Micro QR refusal wording had been changed for every text, not only Kanji, and one edit had dropped a space ("requires M4.Choose"). Both are fixed, and `MicroQr_ErrorDetectionOnlyRefusal_NamesKanjiOnlyForKanji` pins both wordings.
- `spot-check-rmqr` had been broken before this change: its "does it fit behind an ECI header" probe caught an `ArgumentException` that the sizing API stopped throwing when it became `Try`-only, so the first version that could not hold "é" behind an ECI header ended the run. It asks `TryGetRequiredBufferSize` now.
- 6.5 inherits a visible seam: until sets learn Kanji, a text one symbol holds in Kanji but not in UTF-8 comes out as a UTF-8 set of two or more, where `Create` gives one Kanji symbol.

**Trimmed size.** Measured against 6.1 (`27a5caf`, table unreferenced), `PublishTrimmed` with `TrimMode=full`, win-x64: QR encode only 115,200 → 132,608 bytes (+17.0 KB), all three symbologies encoding 178,176 → 197,120 (+18.5 KB), QR decode only 73,216 unchanged. Almost all of it arrived with 6.2, not here: 6.2's writers put the table in reachable mode switches, and a trimmer cannot know that no analysis selected Kanji, so against 6.2 (`c7ee3aa`) this phase adds 0 bytes to QR encode only and 512 to all three. Recorded in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md) beside the table's size.

**Benchmark delta.** Base `c7ee3aa` against this change, both trees exported, ShortRun, three rounds alternating on an idle machine, median of three per arm, 109 arms: the 6.2 set plus `KanjiEncode`, new here (an all-cells text per symbology beside the same text with UTF-8 asked for; the class was copied into the base tree, so base runs today's UTF-8 path). Allocation is identical on every arm. The arms that write Kanji now are faster than both their twins: Standard QR 8 characters 1,001 ns at base → 807 at head, where the head's forced UTF-8 twin takes 972; 320 characters 25.6 → 14.7 µs against 25.6; rMQR 15 characters 381 → 319 ns against 382; Micro QR 184 → 183 ns, where base writes UTF-8 at M4 and head Kanji at M3 (Micro QR has no charset option, so base is its only twin). Class medians of the other arms: `SimpleEncode` -0.6 %, `SimpleMicroQREncode` +1.7 %, `SimpleRmQREncode` +2.3 %, `QRCodeEncodeEndToEnd` +2.8 %, `MicroQREncodeEndToend` +1.2 %, `RmQREncodeEndToEnd` +0.1 %, segmentation classes -0.9 to +2.0 %, except Micro QR `Single` at +7.2 %. The arms past +5 % (every Micro QR `Single` shape, up to +17.4 %; `QR_Byte_V40_H_Encode` +12.5 %; Standard QR `Optimal` alnum-120 +19.8 %; rMQR numeric R7x43 +8.9 %) were measured again with three launches of fifteen iterations, base and head interleaved twice, and all came back between -4.0 and +4.0 % except rMQR numeric R7x43 at +6.0 %. With six launches that arm is the same call with the same text in two classes, and it measured +7.4 % in `SimpleRmQREncode` and -0.8 % in `RmQREncodeEndToEnd`: per-process layout, not a cost on that path, whose only change is the analysis call.

### 6.4 `Optimal` learns Kanji (2026-09-30)

**Done.** An eighth state, Kanji, in a program of its own: `ModeSegmenter.ComputeCostsKanji` (a cost-only loop and one with parents) for a text whose characters are all ASCII or have an encoder cell. An ASCII character reaches Numeric, Alphanumeric and Byte at one byte; a character with a cell reaches only Kanji, since Byte would need an ECI header. After any character either Kanji or the other states are reachable, never both, so Kanji's predecessor takes the byte Byte's takes at an ASCII position: the table stays two bytes a character, and `WalkBack` steps a Kanji run as it steps a Byte run (`CountRuns` gained a Kanji count). The seven-state loops and the lanes are untouched. `TextAnalyzer.Analyze(text, eci, allowKanji, planKanji)` reads past ASCII only when `planKanji` is set, which only the `Optimal` paths do, and marks such a text `KanjiPlannable` on its UTF-8 analysis; `Single` pays nothing new. Each planner branches on the mark into a scan of its own, which takes, below the single-mode (UTF-8) fit, the first candidate a plan holds, the Kanji plan (no ECI header) where both do and the UTF-8 plan otherwise, and returns which one to build (`kanjiPlan`); the generators build it with `TryBuildKanjiPlan` and write it under no charset. Weighing the UTF-8 plan as well was decided here, not in the plan: without it `Optimal` would grow symbols it wrote before, since interleaved kanji and digits pay a header per run as Kanji runs (「1日」×20 then 60 digits: the UTF-8 plan is 7-M, the Kanji plan 8-M). Structured Append sets take no mark (their analysis is the two-argument one), so the lanes, which only sets use, never see the eighth state; that is K9 for now, and 6.5 has to keep it so. `PublicAPI.approved.txt` is unchanged.

Bounds re-derived for the Kanji plan, per the inventory:
- `CheapestSixths` → `CheapestSixthsKanji`: a character with a cell at 78 sixths (13 bits). This is the one screen term that decides: at the UTF-8 rate a kana is 144, and the screen would skip Standard QR's winning version for kana-heavy text and M3 for 「日本語12345」 on Micro QR.
- The header term: the inventory's premise was about the narrowest header (Standard QR's `MinCountBitsAny` stays 8, since Kanji's width at versions 1-9 is 8 too; Micro QR's Kanji header is (version − 1) + version bits; rMQR's 3 + 2). One header in all could not decide for a text the Kanji scan sees, since its plan has a run of each kind. The screens now add a header for every stretch of characters with a cell and every stretch of ASCII (`ModeSegmenter.CheapestSixthsKanji` counts them in the same pass), because no run crosses between them; this was added for speed, after the benchmark (below), and it is tight where each stretch is one run at the narrowest header.
- rMQR: the floor runs at 4 / 3 / 3 / 2 (Kanji's 2 at R7x43 and R11x27), and at 3 it skips 「あい123」, whose Kanji plan fills R7x43-M's 48 bits exactly; the upper bound re-prices the floor plan's Kanji runs; the memo key carries Kanji's width (R13x77 and R15x59 share the other three, as do R13x139 and R17x99); a requested version the single stream does not fit prices the Kanji plan there, since the scan has to say which plan to build.
- `QRSegmentPlanner.PlanCouldBeatSingleMode` / `PlanIsOneByteRun` and the Structured Append premises only Structured Append asks, so they move with 6.5. `CanPlanBeatSingleMode` needs nothing: a plannable text's single mode is Byte.

**Verified.**
- `ModeSegmenterKanjiParityTest`: both loops against `KanjiPlanReference`, an all-states relaxation over eight states written with nothing from the library (a character outside ASCII reaches Kanji only, ASCII classed from the standard's alphabet), on 51 eligible texts (fixed shapes, ties, and a seeded random mix) at every width shape the three planners pass, from rMQR's 4 / 3 / 3 / 2 to Standard QR's 27-40 band: cost, end state, the plan walked back run for run, and the runs counted per mode. The reconstructed plan re-priced equals the program's cost, and the Kanji screen is a lower bound at every width. The seven-state suites (`ModeSegmenter*ParityTest`, the lane and Structured Append walks) pass unchanged.
- `KanjiOptimalTest`, through the public API of all three symbologies: the output equals a reference scan (the first version below the UTF-8 fit that a plan holds, the Kanji plan first; for rMQR every version priced from scratch and ranked by the strategy), where a Kanji plan is written out from `KanjiPlanReference` and `KanjiStreamReference` with the mask pinned and a UTF-8 plan is compared with the same text with UTF-8 asked for; every symbol decodes to its text; the version is never larger than `Single`'s or than the UTF-8 plan's; sizing agrees with `Create`, with the boost too. For each bound that decides, a case where the seven-state bound would have skipped the winning plan: the 13-bit screen (Standard QR, Micro QR), no ECI header on a Kanji plan within 12 bits of its capacity, Kanji's own width in each band, rMQR's 2-bit floor at R7x43, the memo key (R15x59's price handed to R13x77), the requested version, and the boost pricing the Kanji plan. The UTF-8 plan kept where it is smaller (Standard QR, Micro QR 「xЯxЯxЯ12345678」, rMQR), and Kanji taken at a version both fit.
- `KanjiPlanBoundsTest`: each planner's screen, rMQR's floor and upper bound against the optimum at every version, the narrowest widths pinned.
- Existing tests that moved, each an eligible text whose output got smaller: `KanjiEligibilityTest`'s `Optimal` row now expects the Kanji plan where it is smaller (only 「東京タワー333m」, 2-M → 1-M), `RmQRSegmentationTest`'s 「日本語1234567890」 goes R11x43 → R13x27, and its exhaustive reference learned the Kanji plan.
- `tools/mutation_check.cs` planted 41 faults: in the eighth state's loops (each open, continue and cross-mode transition, the first character, the walk back, the run count, the 13-bit width, the screen's 78 sixths), in the analysis (the ASCII clause, the mark, the sizing opt-in), and in each planner and generator (each re-derived bound, the ECI-free pricing, Kanji's widths, the UTF-8 half of each scan, the plan charset, the boost, sizing). All but two are caught. Both are equivalent in the domain the scans see: `Best`'s tie between Kanji and the other states (after any character only one side is reachable), and Micro QR's screen header at 2 × version instead of 2 × version − 1 (the argument in "Done"). The first pass also left Micro QR's UTF-8 half and rMQR's memo key without a test of their own; the key was caught only where a Kanji key collided with a UTF-8 one. `MicroQr_Utf8PlanIsKept_WhereTheKanjiPlanDoesNotFit` and `RmQr_MemoKeyTellsApartVersionsThatShareTheirOtherWidths` catch them, the second with a key that keeps the programs apart but drops Kanji's width.
- `spot-check-microqr` gained four `Optimal` cases (Kanji beside Numeric at M3-L and M3-M, a text no symbol held as UTF-8, and a Byte run of ASCII beside Kanji at M4-L): 18 of 18. `spot-check-rmqr` gained the largest Kanji plan each version and level holds under `Optimal` where UTF-8 cannot (62 of 64; R7x43-H and R11x27-H hold no Kanji plan), and requires zxing-cpp's raw bytes to be its Shift_JIS encoding: 444 of 444. `KanjiZXingCrossTest` has ZXing.Net read Kanji plans in all three Standard QR count bands.
- Byte-identical: the 6.3 harness, rebuilt against each tree (`e6555a6` and this change, each run printing the assembly and MVID it loaded), with the corpus grown by 200 random eligible texts with ASCII in them and the shapes above: 52,716 cases over 754 texts. ASCII, Latin-1, empty, no-cell and all-cells text: 0 differences in 40,154 cases. Eligible text with ASCII: 855 of 12,562 differ, every one under `Optimal` with the charset left to the library (none under `Single`, an explicit charset or a byte order mark), sets only where the set is one symbol. Of the size lines that moved, 265 went to a smaller version and 73 fit where they did not; none grew or stopped fitting (rMQR compared on core modules, by each case's fit strategy). 16 symbols changed at the same version, where the Kanji plan and the UTF-8 plan tie. The same harness against the tree after the speed work below gives the same 52,716 results.
- The speed work below was mutation-checked on its own: 15 faults in the per-stretch screen (each run count, each symbology's header per stretch, the UTF-8 screen's two-byte price), the analysis's ASCII test, and the hoisted widths and payloads in `MeasurePlan`, `PricePlan` and the two writers. All but one are caught. The survivor is equivalent: it tightens Standard QR's UTF-8 screen by one bit, and a UTF-8 plan is weighed only below the single stream's fit, where it has two runs at least and so costs a header more than the screen.

**Trimmed size.** Against `e6555a6`, `PublishTrimmed` with `TrimMode=full`, win-x64: QR encode only 132,608 → 137,216 bytes (+4.5 KB), all three symbologies encoding 197,120 → 204,288 (+7.0 KB), QR decode only 73,216 unchanged, measured after the speed work below. Recorded in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md).

**Lessons.**
- The plan's rule for `Optimal` ("Kanji runs ... taken when it lowers the version, as any plan is today") says nothing about the UTF-8 plan `Optimal` wrote before, and read literally it lets `Optimal` grow a symbol: a Kanji plan pays a header wherever a cell meets ASCII, so interleaved text can lose to one UTF-8 Byte run. Found by pricing 「1日2回3錠」 by hand before writing the scan, and pinned on all three symbologies. The exit criterion "`Optimal` never larger than `Single`" would not have caught it.
- Of the inventory's premises, the per-character price was the only screen term that decides. The narrowest-header terms (Micro QR's count indicator, rMQR's `MinCountBitsAny`) cannot, for the texts the Kanji scans see, because such a plan has at least two runs. So the exit criterion "a test where the old bound would have skipped the winning plan" has nothing to find there, and mutation checking agrees. rMQR's floor width and memo key do decide, and each has its test. The screen worth having for this text is a different one, a header per stretch, and it came from the benchmark, not from the inventory.
- A bound's first test can catch a fault for another reason than the bound. The first catch of the memo-key fault was a Kanji key colliding with a UTF-8 key of the same widths, and a key that keeps the two programs apart but drops Kanji's width went through, until a search under that fault found 「1日」×9 then 28 digits.
- Git Bash's `grep` does not see `\r`, so a CRLF check built on it reported CRLF for files that `sed -i` had turned to LF. `perl` counts them right.
- The seam from 6.3 widens: until 6.5, a text that fits one symbol as a Kanji plan under `Optimal` but not as UTF-8 comes out of `CreateStructuredAppend` as a UTF-8 set of two or more, while `Create` gives one symbol.

**Benchmark delta.** Base `e6555a6` against this change, both trees exported, ShortRun, three rounds alternating, median of three per arm, 152 arms. The set was the 6.3 set plus `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode` (the walk back and the plan pricing changed) and `KanjiEncode`'s new `Optimal` arms: a text with ASCII in it under `Optimal`, beside the same text with UTF-8 asked for, copied into the base tree. That was more than the change could reach; the next phase narrows the set to the classes a change touches, with a few untouched arms for the noise. Allocation is identical on every arm. The untouched arms' class medians are −3.4 % to +1.5 %, overall −0.9 %, except `SimpleEncode` (+10.3 %) and `SimpleMicroQREncode` (+31.5 %). Those two were high in rounds 1 and 3 only and level in round 2, and in the narrowed probe below they came out 8-25 % faster in head, so they are the noise of that run.

The arms whose output moves:
- 「こんにちは世界、QRコードの分割テストです。」×3 as a Kanji plan (7-M, against 10-M) is faster than its UTF-8 twin: 3,140 ns against 3,647.
- 「日本7777」×10 was slower: Standard QR 2,983 ns against the UTF-8 twin's 2,361 (+26 %), rMQR 1,856 against 1,254 (+48 %), and Micro QR 「日本語12345」 322 against base's 261 (+23 %).

Timing each step in Release (Stopwatch, best of nine) showed where the difference was. The Kanji program is cheaper than the UTF-8 one (99 ns against 203 for 60 characters). The difference was:
- the analysis reading past ASCII, with a table lookup on each ASCII character (+90 ns);
- building a plan that wins (270-285 ns), where the UTF-8 twin builds none because its plan loses;
- rMQR's writer at 12-15 ns a run (20 runs here), a third of which was re-measuring the plan.

Three changes followed, all within this phase:
- the analysis tests ASCII before the lookup;
- the screens count a header per stretch (see "Done"), which spares Standard QR the 4-M cost run for this text;
- `MeasurePlan`, `PricePlan` and the Standard QR and rMQR writers look a version's count widths up once instead of per run, which also speeds every existing UTF-8 plan.

By Stopwatch, Standard QR then came out level (2,534 ns against 2,519) and rMQR at +22 % (1,562 against 1,282).

A narrowed probe confirmed it: 24 arms, three launches of fifteen iterations, base and head interleaved twice. The same base arm was 25-50 % apart between that probe's two runs, so each verdict pairs arms of the same run. Standard QR's Kanji plan was within noise of its UTF-8 twin (+5 %), the sentence faster, rMQR +20 %, and Micro QR +30 % against base. What remains on rMQR is a second table lookup per character (the analysis and the writer each look every character up) and a second cost run (the scan's runs keep no predecessors, so the build runs the program again with them). Decided with the user on 2026-09-30: that work goes to 6.8, which therefore lands before the release; the row above says so.
